title: Truth, Order, and Faithful Elders
summary: Paul grounds Titus’s mission in God’s unfailing promise, sets out the character required of Cretan elders, and exposes teachers whose conduct denies the God they profess.
historicalContext: Crete, a long mountainous island south of the Aegean, had been a Roman province for more than a century when Paul wrote. Its towns were numerous, its Jewish community sizable, and its people carried an old reputation for dishonesty and greed that even their own writers acknowledged. Cretans had heard the gospel at Pentecost, and Paul’s later ministry there, apparently after his release from his first Roman imprisonment, left believing groups in several cities. Paul departed before the work was complete, leaving Titus, an uncircumcised Gentile convert and a seasoned troubleshooter from the Corinthian crisis, to organize the congregations. The situation was urgent: teachers with a Jewish orientation were spreading myths, purity rules of human origin, and arguments that unsettled whole households, and some were doing it for money. Into this setting Paul writes a compact, practical letter meant to be read in the churches as well as by Titus himself.
literaryContext: The opening chapter moves from foundation to structure to defense. An unusually full salutation (1:1–4) states the purpose of Paul’s apostleship—faith, knowledge of truth, and godliness resting on the hope of eternal life—and so introduces vocabulary that runs through the whole letter. Paul then restates Titus’s commission and lists the qualities that must mark elders, who are also called overseers and God’s stewards (1:5–9). The final requirement, holding fast the faithful word in order to exhort and refute, opens directly onto a portrait of the opponents (1:10–16): rebellious talkers of the circumcision party, motivated by gain, devoted to myths and human commandments, and claiming to know God while their works deny Him. The chapter’s contrast between truth that produces godliness and profession that produces nothing good prepares for chapter 2, where Titus is to teach what befits sound doctrine.
themes: Hope resting on the God who cannot lie
Character as the qualification for oversight
Sound teaching that heals and corrects

outline.title: An Apostle’s Greeting and Purpose
outline.summary: Paul describes his commission as serving the faith, knowledge, and godliness of God’s people, anchored in God’s eternal promise and entrusted to him by command.

outline.title: Appointing Elders in Every City
outline.summary: Titus is to complete the organization of the Cretan churches by appointing blameless elders whose homes, temperament, virtues, and grip on the word fit them to serve as God’s stewards.

outline.title: Silencing Deceivers and Rebuking the Wayward
outline.summary: Many rebellious teachers, driven by gain, are upsetting households; their mouths must be stopped and those influenced must be sharply corrected for the sake of sound faith.

outline.title: Purity of Heart and the Test of Works
outline.summary: Purity resides in a cleansed heart rather than in human rituals, and those whose minds are defiled reveal by their deeds that their claim to know God is empty.

verses.bibleText: Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul opens this letter with a self-description he uses nowhere else: “a servant of God.” In other greetings he calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. Here the wording reaches back to the language Israel’s Scriptures used for Moses, Joshua, David, and the prophets, people who belonged wholly to the Lord and spoke at His bidding. Joined at once to “an apostle of Jesus Christ,” the double title holds lowliness and commission together. Paul claims no independent standing, owns nothing in himself, and yet arrives bearing the authority of the risen Lord who met him outside Damascus and sent him to the nations.

The fullness of this greeting, written to a trusted co-worker, serves a practical end. Titus was laboring in a young and unsettled field where his instructions would be questioned and resisted. A letter opening with so complete a statement of Paul’s credentials would be read aloud in the Cretan congregations, and its hearers would understand that Titus acted under apostolic direction. To set aside his counsel would be to set aside the man who sent him, and beyond Paul, the Lord who commissioned Paul.

“According to the faith of God’s elect” most naturally states the aim of the apostleship: Paul serves in order to bring forth and strengthen faith among those whom God has chosen. “Elect” recalls Israel, the people called to carry God’s saving purpose to the world. That calling now rests on the community gathered around Christ, Jew and Gentile together. In Paul’s usage election is God’s gracious initiative, answered as people hear the gospel and believe; it never makes preaching unnecessary.

Faith is paired with “the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness.” The knowledge in view is personal recognition and embrace of gospel truth, and that truth has a recognizable direction. It produces godliness, a life that reverences God and reflects Him in ordinary conduct. The phrase anticipates the entire letter. Crete’s false teachers would claim to know God while living disorderly lives (1:16). From the first line Paul insists that truth rightly received cannot be separated from the character it forms.

wordNotes.term: δοῦλος θεοῦ (doulos theou) — a servant of God
wordNotes.explanation: In ordinary Greek a doulos was a slave, owned by a master and answerable to him alone. Paul usually qualifies the word with “of Jesus Christ”; the phrase “of God” here echoes the Old Testament habit of calling Israel’s leaders and prophets the Lord’s servants. The title therefore unites complete belonging with honored commission: the servant has no rights of his own, yet he speaks for the Master.

wordNotes.term: ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας τῆς κατ’ εὐσέβειαν (epignōsin alētheias tēs kat’ eusebeian) — the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness
wordNotes.explanation: Epignōsis denotes recognition and personal grasp of something, here the truth of the gospel. The qualifying phrase identifies the kind of truth meant: truth that accords with and leads to eusebeia, reverent devotion to God expressed in a godly manner of life. Doctrine and conduct belong together in the Pastoral Letters, and this opening phrase states the principle concisely.

verses.bibleText: In hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s apostolic labor rests “in hope of eternal life.” The preposition pictures hope as the ground on which the whole work stands. Biblical hope is confident expectation anchored in what God has said, waiting for what is promised but not yet seen.

Eternal life is the life of the age to come, given by God through Jesus Christ. Scripture does not describe it as something human beings possess by nature. It is promised, received now by faith as a present relationship with God and a pledge of what is coming, and granted in its fullness when Christ appears and those who sleep in Him are raised. Titus 2:13 and 3:7 develop the same expectation: believers are heirs “according to the hope of eternal life,” watching for “the glorious appearing” of their Saviour.

The guarantee lies in the character of the One who made the promise. “God, that cannot lie” renders a single Greek adjective meaning free from falsehood. The thought is rooted in Israel’s confession that God is not a man that He should lie (Numbers 23:19). Set beside the Cretan proverb about liars (1:12), the contrast is pointed. The security of these young believers depends on no human word, however eloquent, but on the God whose word cannot fail.

“Before the world began” reads more literally “before times eternal.” Paul looks back beyond history to God’s eternal purpose. The promise of life was not improvised after sin entered the world; redemption belongs to the counsel of God before the ages (2 Timothy 1:9). A hope that begins in God’s eternal intention and rests on His truthfulness cannot be overturned by local disorder, opposition, or delay.

wordNotes.term: ἀψευδής (apseudēs) — that cannot lie
wordNotes.explanation: This adjective occurs only here in the New Testament. Formed from the word for falsehood with a negating prefix, it describes God as entirely without deceit. The same conviction is expressed elsewhere when Scripture declares it impossible for God to lie. Paul places the term beside the promise of eternal life to show that the hope rests on God’s own unchanging truthfulness.

wordNotes.term: πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων (pro chronōn aiōniōn) — before the world began
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “before times eternal,” the phrase reaches behind the ages of history to God’s purpose before creation. Paul uses the same expression of the grace given in Christ, which was then made manifest at His appearing. The pattern is eternal purpose followed by revelation in time, which is exactly the movement from this verse to the next.

verses.bibleText: But hath in due times manifested his word through preaching, which is committed unto me according to the commandment of God our Saviour;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 3 moves from eternity to history. The promise God made before the ages “hath in due times” been brought into the open. The plural “times” refers to the season God judged fitting, the moment He appointed for disclosing His saving purpose in the coming, death, and resurrection of His Son. Paul says the same elsewhere: “when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4).

What God manifested is “his word,” the message of salvation that tells of eternal life in Christ. That word reaches people “through preaching,” a term for the public announcement made by a herald. Paul sees no gap between God’s revelation and the apostolic proclamation of it. When the gospel is faithfully preached, God Himself is making His word known.

The proclamation “is committed unto me,” Paul writes, with an emphatic “I.” He never lost his astonishment that the former persecutor had been entrusted with the gospel. The trust was not self-chosen; it came “according to the commandment of God our Saviour.” Paul’s ministry was obedience to an order, and the burden of it pressed on him so heavily that he could say, “woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!”

The title “God our Saviour” recurs in this letter (2:10; 3:4) and presents the Father as the source and initiator of salvation. For Cretans who had grown up with gods of myth and with rulers who claimed the title “saviour,” the phrase made a clear claim: deliverance from sin comes from the one living God, who has now spoken through His appointed messengers.

wordNotes.term: καιροῖς ἰδίοις (kairois idiois) — in due times
wordNotes.explanation: Kairos often refers to a fitting or decisive moment rather than to time as duration. With idios, “its own,” the phrase means the time that properly belonged to God’s plan. Paul uses similar wording for the testimony of Christ’s self-giving and for His future appearing, both set by God’s own timing.

wordNotes.term: κήρυγμα (kērygma) — preaching
wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes the proclamation of a herald, an official announcement made publicly on behalf of a sovereign. In the New Testament it describes the content and act of gospel preaching. Paul regards this apparently weak means as the instrument God chose to save those who believe.

verses.bibleText: To Titus, mine own son after the common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter is addressed “To Titus, mine own son after the common faith.” Titus is never named in Acts, but Paul’s letters show him to be one of the apostle’s most dependable associates. He traveled with Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem, where as an uncircumcised Greek he became a test case for the freedom of Gentile believers (Galatians 2:1–3). Later he handled the delicate and strained relationship with the Corinthian church, organized the collection there, and brought Paul news that refreshed him (2 Corinthians 7:6–7; 8:6, 23). Paul’s confidence in him on Crete grew out of proven service.

“Mine own son” describes a true spiritual child, perhaps one brought to faith through Paul, certainly one formed by his teaching. The faith that binds them is “common,” shared alike by the Jewish apostle and the Gentile convert. In a letter that will confront teachers “of the circumcision” (1:10), the word is significant. Titus did not need circumcision or any added ritual to belong fully to God’s people; he stood on the same footing of grace as Paul himself.

The blessing follows Paul’s usual pattern. Many early manuscripts read only “Grace and peace,” though the KJV, with other copies, includes “mercy” as in the letters to Timothy. Grace is God’s unearned favor; peace is the wholeness and reconciliation it brings. Both come “from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour.” Having just called God “our Saviour” (1:3), Paul now gives the same title to Christ. The Father plans and the Son accomplishes one salvation, and the letter will repeatedly place the two side by side (2:10, 13; 3:4, 6).

wordNotes.term: γνησίῳ τέκνῳ (gnēsiō teknō) — mine own son
wordNotes.explanation: Gnēsios described a legitimate child, born within marriage, and so came to mean true or genuine. Paul uses it of Timothy in the same way and of a loyal co-worker at Philippi. The title affirms the authenticity of Titus’s relationship to Paul and therefore of the authority he carries in Crete.

wordNotes.term: κοινὴν πίστιν (koinēn pistin) — the common faith
wordNotes.explanation: Koinos means shared or held in common. The faith Paul and Titus share belongs equally to Jewish and Gentile believers. The same idea underlies the confession that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, and Jude speaks similarly of a salvation held in common by all the saints.

verses.bibleText: For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “For this cause left I thee in Crete” Paul moves straight to business. The verb means to leave someone behind, implying that Paul and Titus had worked on the island together. Acts records only a brief stop at Crete during Paul’s voyage as a prisoner, so this mission most likely belongs to the years after his release from the first Roman imprisonment. The gospel had evidently taken root in several towns, but Paul had to move on before the believers were properly organized.

Titus was to “set in order the things that are wanting.” The work was partly corrective and partly a matter of completion: straightening what had gone crooked and supplying what had not yet been put in place. Chief among those needs was leadership. Titus must “ordain elders in every city,” following the pattern Paul and Barnabas had used in Galatia, where they appointed elders in every church with prayer and fasting (Acts 14:23). The plural suggests a body of elders for each local congregation rather than a single ruler.

“As I had appointed thee” recalls instructions Paul had already given in person. Repeating them in writing gave Titus a document he could show the churches. Some in Crete may have resented the arrival of structure, or may have preferred the influence of self-appointed teachers. The letter made it plain that the arrangement came from the apostle.

The verse shows that order is no enemy of spiritual life. Young believers needed shepherds who would teach, guard, and model the faith. A church without recognized, qualified leadership is exposed to every persuasive voice, and Crete already had many such voices (1:10). Paul’s remedy was neither a rigid hierarchy nor a vacuum, but faithful elders chosen by clear standards.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιδιορθώσῃ (epidiorthōsē) — thou shouldest set in order
wordNotes.explanation: This compound verb appears only here in the Bible. Its root speaks of straightening or setting right, and the added prefix suggests carrying the correction further, completing what had been begun. Titus was not founding the Cretan churches but finishing the work of putting them on a sound footing, so that all things might be done decently and in order.

wordNotes.term: πρεσβυτέρους (presbyterous) — elders
wordNotes.explanation: The term was familiar from synagogue life, where respected senior men guided the community. In the church it became the title of recognized leaders who shepherd and oversee a congregation. Here it designates an office, as the qualifications that follow make clear, and the same men are called overseers in verse 7.

verses.bibleText: If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The qualifications begin with a conditional clause, “If any be blameless,” implying that whoever meets these standards may be appointed. Blamelessness heads the list and governs the rest. The word describes a person against whom no legitimate charge can be brought. It does not demand sinless perfection, which no candidate could offer, but a settled pattern of life that gives neither the church nor outsiders grounds for accusation. In Crete, where moral reputation was poor and the opponents eager for ammunition, this mattered greatly.

“The husband of one wife” is literally “a man of one woman.” The phrase requires marital and sexual faithfulness. In a culture where concubines, casual unions, and easy divorce were common, an elder had to be wholly devoted to his wife. The expression assumes that most candidates would be married, but its thrust is fidelity rather than a requirement to marry or to have children. An unmarried man of pure life is no more excluded than a man without children is excluded by the next clause.

The household is the next proving ground. The elder should have “faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.” The adjective can mean “believing” or “faithful” in the sense of trustworthy and obedient. The phrase that follows explains it in terms of behavior: the children must not be open to the charge of dissolute living or rebellious defiance.

The parallel requirement in 1 Timothy 3:4–5 reasons that a man unable to lead his own family is unfit to care for the church of God. The concern is children still under their father’s roof and authority, and the standard is what every Christian home should aim at.

The tragedy of Eli, whose sons disgraced the sanctuary while he failed to restrain them, shows how a leader’s domestic neglect can damage a whole people. Paul’s standard remains practical for every congregation today. The home reveals whether a man’s faith governs his closest relationships, and those relationships are the first place where his capacity to shepherd others becomes visible.

wordNotes.term: ἀνέγκλητος (anenklētos) — blameless
wordNotes.explanation: Built from a verb meaning to bring a charge against, the word describes someone not open to accusation. It is used of deacons in 1 Timothy and of the condition in which Christ presents believers before God. In leadership lists it refers to an observable reputation for integrity, not to an absence of all imperfection.

wordNotes.term: μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ (mias gynaikos anēr) — the husband of one wife
wordNotes.explanation: The Greek places “one” first for emphasis: a one-woman man. The phrase calls for exclusive faithfulness within marriage, reflecting the Creator’s design that a man cleave to his wife and the two become one flesh. A matching phrase describes the widow enrolled for church support as the wife of one man.

verses.bibleText: For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now uses a second title for the same office. “A bishop,” more precisely an overseer, names what the elder does: he watches over the flock. The two words are interchangeable in the New Testament, as the move from “elders” in verse 5 to “bishop” here shows, and as Paul’s address to the Ephesian elders confirms when he tells them the Holy Spirit made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28). The later distinction between a bishop over many churches and the elders of a congregation does not appear in this text.

Blamelessness is repeated, this time with a reason: the overseer serves “as the steward of God.” A steward managed a household or estate on behalf of its owner. He held real authority, but every decision belonged to his master and would one day be reviewed. The church is God’s household (1 Timothy 3:15). Those who care for it handle what belongs to Him and are answerable to Him, which is why their character must bear inspection.

Five negatives follow, each describing a way in which self can seize control. He must not be “selfwilled,” stubbornly pleasing himself and dismissive of others. He must not be “soon angry,” a man whose temper flares when he is crossed. He must not be “given to wine,” ruled by drink; Scripture’s repeated warnings against wine’s deceptive power (Proverbs 20:1; 23:29–32) commend complete freedom from its hold. He must be “no striker,” never a bully who settles conflict by force or intimidation. And he must not be “given to filthy lucre,” using his position for gain.

The list is realistic. Pride, temper, appetite, aggression, and greed have ruined ministries in every century. A steward who indulges any of them begins to treat God’s household as his own possession, and the flock pays the price. The positive qualities in verse 8 supply the remedy.

wordNotes.term: οἰκονόμος θεοῦ (oikonomos theou) — the steward of God
wordNotes.explanation: An oikonomos was a household manager, often a trusted slave, who oversaw property and servants for his master. Jesus used the figure for faithful servants awaiting their lord’s return, and Paul applied it to ministers entrusted with the mysteries of God. The defining requirement of a steward is faithfulness to the owner.

wordNotes.term: αὐθάδης (authadēs) — selfwilled
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes a person who is self-pleasing and obstinate, intent on his own way and indifferent to the views or needs of others. Peter uses it of presumptuous false teachers who despise authority. In a leader it produces a domineering spirit, the opposite of the example Peter commends to elders.

verses.bibleText: But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Against the five vices Paul sets six virtues. The overseer must be “a lover of hospitality,” opening his home to believers and travelers. In a world without safe public lodging, and with churches meeting in houses, hospitality was a practical necessity and a visible expression of love. He must also be “a lover of good men,” better rendered “a lover of what is good.” His affections are drawn toward goodness in people, actions, and things.

He must be “sober,” sound-minded and self-possessed, with balanced judgment. He must be “just,” dealing uprightly with others in a way that accords with God’s law, and “holy,” devout and pleasing to God. The pairing reaches in two directions, toward neighbor and toward God, and these two specifically religious qualities do not appear in the parallel list in 1 Timothy 3.

The list closes with “temperate,” a word for self-mastery. It caps the positive qualities just as blamelessness headed the whole list. The temperate person governs appetite, desire, and impulse rather than being governed by them. Paul names this quality among the fruit of the Spirit and compares it to the discipline of an athlete who keeps his body under control so that he will not be disqualified.

None of these qualities is extraordinary. Paul does not require eloquence, wealth, or charisma. He asks for the ordinary graces of a Christian life, matured and proven. Leaders are to show clearly what every believer is called to be, so that the congregation sees in them a living picture of the gospel’s power.

wordNotes.term: φιλόξενον, φιλάγαθον (philoxenon, philagathon) — a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men
wordNotes.explanation: Both adjectives begin with phil-, expressing affection. Philoxenos means fond of strangers, hence hospitable; philagathos, found only here in the New Testament, means devoted to the good. The second need not be limited to good people, as the KJV suggests; it describes a heart attracted to whatever is excellent and praiseworthy.

wordNotes.term: ἐγκρατῆ (enkratē) — temperate
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes one who has power over himself. Its noun form appears in the fruit of the Spirit and in Paul’s reasoning before Felix about righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come. Temperance in Scripture includes control of appetite and passion and reaches to every area of life.

verses.bibleText: Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The final qualification concerns the elder’s relationship to the truth. He must be “holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught.” The verb means to cling to something firmly and devote oneself to it. The “faithful word” is the reliable message of the gospel, and it is reliable because it accords with what the apostles taught. An elder does not invent his own message. He receives, guards, and passes on what was delivered, as Paul instructed Timothy to entrust what he had heard to faithful men who would teach others (2 Timothy 2:2).

The purpose follows: “that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.” The elder has two tasks. He must encourage and urge the congregation in healthy teaching, building them up in faith and practice. And he must answer those who speak against the truth, exposing their errors so that their influence is checked. Both tasks require the same equipment: a firm, informed grasp of Scripture.

“Sound doctrine” is healthy teaching. The medical image runs through the Pastoral Letters, where false teaching spreads like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17) and the truth brings spiritual health. An elder must therefore be a diligent student of the Word. Good intentions cannot make up for ignorance of Scripture, and a leader who misunderstands the Bible may bend its words to fit his own ideas and lead others astray. The God-breathed Scriptures, Paul reminds Timothy, thoroughly equip the servant of God for every good work.

The word “convince” carries the idea of bringing an error to light so clearly that it stands exposed. The goal is not winning arguments for their own sake. Paul hopes that opponents may come to repentance and recover themselves (2 Timothy 2:25–26). Firm conviction and patient gentleness belong together in the elder’s work.

wordNotes.term: ὑγιαινούσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ (hygiainousē didaskalia) — sound doctrine
wordNotes.explanation: The participle comes from the verb “to be healthy,” the root of the English word hygiene. Sound doctrine is teaching that promotes spiritual health, in contrast to error that sickens and corrupts. The phrase recurs in the Pastoral Letters as a name for the apostolic gospel and its moral implications.

wordNotes.term: ἐλέγχειν (elenchein) — to convince
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to bring something into the light so that it is exposed and shown for what it is, and from there to refute, convict, or reprove. Jesus uses it of the Spirit’s work of convicting the world of sin. The same verb returns in verse 13, where Titus is told to rebuke sharply.

verses.bibleText: For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The connecting “For” explains why elders must be able to refute opposition: “there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers.” The problem was not one stray voice but a crowd. These people were “unruly,” refusing to submit to God’s word or to the order of the church; Paul applies the same word to rebellious children in verse 6. They were “vain talkers,” producing a flood of speech without substance. And they were “deceivers,” leading minds astray, quite possibly having first deceived themselves.

The most influential among them were “they of the circumcision,” believers of Jewish background who pressed Jewish traditions on Gentile converts. Crete had a large Jewish population, and Cretans were among those in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), so a mixed church was natural. Paul himself was a Jew and loved his people. His objection was to teaching that added human requirements to the gospel and treated Gentile believers like Titus as second-class (Galatians 2:3–5, 12).

The description warns every generation. Error often arrives with confident talk, an appeal to tradition, and a refusal to be accountable. Its persuasive power lies less in the strength of its arguments than in the volume and persistence of its advocates. Faithful leaders must therefore know the truth well enough to recognize empty words when they hear them.

wordNotes.term: ματαιολόγοι καὶ φρεναπάται (mataiologoi kai phrenapatai) — vain talkers and deceivers
wordNotes.explanation: Both compounds are rare. Mataiologos joins “empty” and “speaking” to describe someone whose talk has no profitable content; Paul warns elsewhere of those who have turned aside to vain jangling. Phrenapatēs combines “mind” and “deceive,” a person who leads minds astray. Paul uses the related verb of one who deceives himself by thinking he is something when he is nothing.

wordNotes.term: οἱ ἐκ τῆς περιτομῆς (hoi ek tēs peritomēs) — they of the circumcision
wordNotes.explanation: The expression identifies people of Jewish origin and, in the New Testament, usually Jewish believers. It can be neutral, as when Paul names faithful co-workers of the circumcision, but it often describes those who insisted that Gentiles adopt Jewish customs, as in the controversy at Antioch.

verses.bibleText: Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s verdict is firm: their “mouths must be stopped.” The verb pictures putting a bridle or muzzle on an animal. The church cannot give such teachers a platform. Paul does not prescribe violence or civil penalties. The means are those he has already named: elders who can refute error with sound teaching (1:9), sharp rebuke (1:13), and, if warnings are refused, separation from the fellowship (3:10–11).

The urgency comes from the damage being done. These teachers “subvert whole houses.” Since congregations met in homes, upsetting a household could unsettle an entire church. Families were being turned from the faith, perhaps divided as some members embraced the new teaching and others resisted it. Similar teachers at Ephesus worked their way into homes and captivated the vulnerable (2 Timothy 3:6).

They were “teaching things which they ought not,” and their motive was “filthy lucre’s sake.” Paul affirms elsewhere that those who labor in the word deserve support (1 Timothy 5:17–18). The shame lay in turning religion into a source of profit and shaping the message to keep income flowing. The same vice appears among the disqualifications for elders in verse 7, which shows how directly the requirements answer the Cretan crisis. Whenever money becomes the hidden engine of a ministry, the content of its teaching will eventually bend to serve it. Paul’s concern for financial integrity in leaders protects the gospel itself.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιστομίζειν (epistomizein) — must be stopped
wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, the verb literally means to put something over the mouth, as with a bit or muzzle. James uses the image of bits in horses’ mouths to describe controlling the whole body. The point is to prevent harmful speech from spreading, using the church’s spiritual means of truth and discipline.

wordNotes.term: αἰσχροῦ κέρδους χάριν (aischrou kerdous charin) — for filthy lucre’s sake
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “for the sake of shameful gain.” The gain is disgraceful because it is obtained by teaching error and because profit has become the purpose of ministry. Peter urges elders to shepherd willingly and not for such gain, and Paul warns of those who suppose that gain is godliness.

verses.bibleText: One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now cites a line the Cretans knew well: “One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said, The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.” The saying was widely attributed to Epimenides of Knossos, a sixth-century BC poet and seer whom many Cretans honored with almost legendary reverence. Paul calls him a prophet because that is how his own people regarded him, not because Paul thought him inspired. He quoted Greek poets on other occasions as well, at Athens and in writing to Corinth (Acts 17:28; 1 Corinthians 15:33).

The line was proverbial. Greek even had a verb meaning “to play the Cretan,” that is, to lie. “Evil beasts” suggests savage, untamed behavior, and “slow bellies” describes lazy gluttons who live for appetite. Other ancient writers likewise criticized the island’s reputation for greed.

This verse must be read with care. Paul does not single out an ethnic group as uniquely depraved, nor does he teach that a person’s birthplace determines his character. His aim is the conduct of the false teachers and those they were swaying. Each part of the proverb matches what he has just described: lying corresponds to the “deceivers” (1:10), brutishness to those who overturn households (1:11), and greedy appetite to teaching “for filthy lucre’s sake.” By quoting a Cretan rather than an outsider, Paul lets the island’s own proverb expose behavior that the troublemakers were displaying, and he spares himself the charge of prejudice.

The rest of the letter confirms this reading. Cretan believers are among “God’s elect” (1:1) and share “the common faith” (1:4). Paul includes himself in the old life of folly and lust (3:3) and celebrates the kindness of God that saves people of every background (3:4–5). Every culture has characteristic sins, and every one of them stands in need of the same grace. The gospel never regards any people as beyond redemption. It calls each person, whatever his heritage, to put away the sins that mark his surroundings and to show instead the character of Christ.

wordNotes.term: ἴδιος αὐτῶν προφήτης (idios autōn prophētēs) — a prophet of their own
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled possessive, literally “their own prophet,” stresses that the speaker was a Cretan regarded by Cretans as a seer. This is the only place in Scripture where a pagan writer is called a prophet, and the title reflects the people’s estimate rather than divine inspiration. Paul could use the words of non-Christian poets when a familiar line served his point.

wordNotes.term: ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί (pseustai, kaka thēria, gasteres argai) — liars, evil beasts, slow bellies
wordNotes.explanation: The three terms describe dishonesty, wild and harmful behavior, and idle appetite. Gastēr, belly, stands for the whole person viewed as governed by appetite, so the phrase means lazy gluttons. Paul speaks elsewhere of those whose god is their belly and of teachers who serve their own belly rather than Christ, linking false teaching with self-indulgence.

verses.bibleText: This witness is true. Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“This witness is true.” Paul affirms that the proverb accurately describes the behavior confronting Titus. He does not claim that every Cretan was dishonest. A proverb names a recognizable pattern, and that pattern was now showing up inside the church through the troublemakers and those drawn after them. Titus needed to see his situation clearly rather than hope the problem would fade.

“Wherefore rebuke them sharply.” The verb is the same one used in verse 9 for refuting gainsayers. The adverb comes from a word meaning to cut off, and suggests a decisive, unambiguous correction. Mild suggestions would not reach people who had grown comfortable with deception and greed. The rebuke is directed at those spreading or embracing the error, not at the Cretan population as a whole.

The purpose shows the heart behind the severity: “that they may be sound in the faith.” Paul aims at health. His sharpness is a surgeon’s incision made in order to heal, not a blow struck to wound. In writing to Corinth he used the same adverb and explained that his authority was given for building up, not for tearing down (2 Corinthians 13:10). Church discipline in Scripture is always remedial in intent.

Those who correct others must therefore examine their own motives. Firmness that seeks restoration reflects Christ; harshness that seeks to humiliate does not. When a rebuke is given with the aim of recovering the person to sound faith, it becomes an act of love.

wordNotes.term: ἀποτόμως (apotomōs) — sharply
wordNotes.explanation: The adverb derives from a verb meaning to cut off abruptly. It describes speech that is direct and severe. Paul uses it once more, of the sharpness he hoped not to need at Corinth, and the related noun describes the severity of God toward those who persist in unbelief, set beside His goodness.

wordNotes.term: ὑγιαίνωσιν ἐν τῇ πίστει (hygiainōsin en tē pistei) — sound in the faith
wordNotes.explanation: The verb “to be healthy” returns from verse 9. Here it describes people who hold the apostolic faith in a healthy, uncorrupted form. The older men of the congregation are to be sound in faith as well, and Paul contrasts wholesome words with the sickly obsession of false teachers over questions.

verses.bibleText: Not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Being sound in the faith requires turning away from two kinds of error. The first is “Jewish fables,” imaginative legends spun from Old Testament genealogies and stories. Paul warns Timothy about the same kind of material, myths and endless genealogies that breed questions rather than godly edifying (1 Timothy 1:4), and later tells Titus to avoid foolish questions and genealogies (3:9).

The second is “commandments of men, that turn from the truth.” The phrase recalls Isaiah’s rebuke of worship taught by human precept, which Jesus applied to traditions that set aside God’s command (Matthew 15:3–9). Paul’s target is human regulation: ascetic rules and purity customs invented by teachers and imposed as conditions of holiness (Colossians 2:20–22). He is not opposing the law of God, which he calls holy, just, and good. Jesus made the same distinction, holding fast the commandment of God while exposing traditions that displaced it.

The teachers who promote such rules are people who “turn from the truth.” The safeguard for the church is close attention to Scripture itself, so that God’s commands are honored and human inventions are recognized for what they are.

wordNotes.term: Ἰουδαϊκοῖς μύθοις (Ioudaikois mythois) — Jewish fables
wordNotes.explanation: Mythos denotes a story or legend, and in the New Testament always something set against the truth. Peter insists that the apostles did not follow cunningly devised fables when they made known Christ’s power and coming. The adjective here identifies the source of these tales in Jewish speculative tradition rather than in Scripture.

wordNotes.term: ἐντολαῖς ἀνθρώπων (entolais anthrōpōn) — commandments of men
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase echoes Isaiah’s complaint that the people’s reverence was taught by human precept. Jesus quoted the passage against traditions that nullified God’s word, and Paul used similar language of ascetic rules. In each case the contrast is between what God commands and what people add.

verses.bibleText: Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure; but even their mind and conscience is defiled.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul answers the purity rules of verse 14 with a principle: “Unto the pure all things are pure.” “The pure” are those whose hearts have been cleansed by God through faith in Christ. Peter told the Jerusalem council that God purified the hearts of Gentile believers by faith (Acts 15:9), and this letter will say that Christ gave Himself to purify a people for His own (2:14). For people cleansed in that way, the things God has made and given for human use are not contaminated by contact, by the hands that prepared them, or by the absence of some ceremonial washing invented by men.

The context determines the scope of “all things.” Paul is answering “commandments of men” (1:14), not commandments of God. The purity regulations at issue were human additions: ascetic prohibitions, ritual washings, and taboos that made holiness depend on external observance. The parallel in 1 Timothy 4:3–5 speaks of foods God created to be received with thanksgiving and sanctified by His word, that is, foods His word identifies as fit for eating.

The verse therefore does not abolish the distinction between clean and unclean foods that God Himself set out in Leviticus 11, a distinction already known in Noah’s day (Genesis 7:2). Paul’s similar statement that “all things are lawful” (1 Corinthians 6:12) plainly does not permit what Scripture forbids, and this one should be read with the same care.

The second half of the verse turns the principle around: “unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure.” Where the heart is unclean, everything it touches is affected. Haggai made the same point when he showed that holiness does not spread by contact but uncleanness does (Haggai 2:11–14). No ritual can purify a person whose inner life is corrupt. Jesus taught that what defiles a man comes from within, from the heart (Mark 7:20–23).

The deepest problem is that “even their mind and conscience is defiled.” Their way of thinking and their moral sense have both been corrupted. A conscience in that state can no longer be trusted to tell right from wrong. The false teachers could be scrupulous about rules while blind to deceit and greed. The remedy is the cleansing of the heart by Christ, out of which flows an obedience that honors everything God has actually commanded.

wordNotes.term: καθαροῖς (katharois) — unto the pure
wordNotes.explanation: Katharos means clean or pure, and here it has its moral and spiritual sense: those inwardly cleansed. Jesus pronounced a blessing on the pure in heart, and Paul describes the goal of his charge as love out of a pure heart. The word in this clause describes people, while the following “all things are pure” speaks of what they use.

wordNotes.term: ὁ νοῦς καὶ ἡ συνείδησις (ho nous kai hē syneidēsis) — mind and conscience
wordNotes.explanation: Nous refers to the mind as one’s way of thinking and judging; syneidēsis is the inner awareness that approves or condemns one’s conduct. When both are defiled, a person can neither see truly nor feel rightly about right and wrong. Scripture speaks of a conscience seared and of a mind needing renewal, and points to Christ’s blood as the power that purges the conscience.

verses.bibleText: They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul closes with a verdict on the opponents: “They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him.” They claimed special knowledge of God. Their conduct told another story.

Three severe words follow. They are “abominable,” detestable in God’s sight. The irony is sharp: people preoccupied with avoiding defilement had themselves become loathsome to God. They are “disobedient,” refusing the very truth they professed to teach. And they are “unto every good work reprobate,” a word for metal or coins that fail the test and are rejected as worthless.

The verse sets up the rest of the letter, which repeatedly calls believers to good works (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). The contrast is not between faith and works as rival ways of salvation. Titus 3:5 will insist that God saves by mercy, not by works of righteousness. The contrast lies between a living faith that bears fruit and a hollow profession that bears none. John states the principle plainly: whoever claims to know God but does not keep His commandments is a liar (1 John 2:4). Words about God cost little. A life shaped by His truth is the evidence that one actually knows Him.

wordNotes.term: ἀδόκιμοι (adokimoi) — reprobate
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes what has been tested and found wanting, such as counterfeit coin or flawed metal. Paul urges the Corinthians to examine themselves lest they prove reprobate, and he disciplined his own body lest he be disqualified. Here the opponents are unfit for any good work.

wordNotes.term: βδελυκτοί (bdeluktoi) — abominable
wordNotes.explanation: This adjective, used only here in the New Testament, belongs to the word family the Greek Old Testament uses for things abhorrent to God. Jesus warned that what is highly esteemed among people can be an abomination in God’s sight, and Proverbs calls the one who justifies the wicked abominable to the Lord.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would you look for first if you had to choose leaders for a young church surrounded by confusion and false teaching?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God’s truth, resting on His unfailing promise, produces godly character; the church therefore needs leaders whose lives and teaching embody that truth and who can correct those whose works deny it.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul tie the knowledge of truth so closely to godliness in the opening verse?
What do the qualifications in verses 6–8 reveal about how God measures fitness for leadership?
Why must an elder be able both to encourage with sound teaching and to refute opposition?
How can a church correct error firmly while still aiming at the restoration of those who err?
In what ways can a person’s works deny the God his words confess?
commonMisunderstandings: Blameless does not mean sinless; it describes a life against which no serious, legitimate charge can be sustained.
The quotation about Cretans is not a license for ethnic contempt; Paul uses a saying the Cretans knew in order to expose conduct the false teachers were displaying.

“Unto the pure all things are pure” does not erase the distinctions God Himself drew in Scripture, such as the clean and unclean foods of Leviticus 11; it rejects human purity rules that replace inner cleansing.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep doctrine and life together throughout: the truth Paul preaches leads to godliness, elders are qualified chiefly by character, and false teaching is finally exposed by the works it produces.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Rest your hope on the God who cannot lie, and ask Him to make your life an honest confirmation of the truth you profess.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The God who cannot lie promised eternal life before the ages and has revealed it in the gospel; receiving that truth brings faith that becomes godly living.
flow: God made a promise of life before the world began, and His character guarantees it.
In the fullness of time He revealed that promise in the gospel of Jesus Christ, our Saviour.
The gospel calls for faith and a personal acknowledgment of the truth.
Truth received by faith produces a life of godliness, unlike religion that is all profession.
Eternal life is God’s gift, awaited in hope and given in fullness at Christ’s appearing.
simpleIllustrations: A promise is only as dependable as the one who makes it; a signed guarantee from a known liar is worthless, but God’s word is backed by His unchanging truthfulness.
A fruit tree is known by what grows on its branches, not by the label tied to its trunk; profession is tested by fruit.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you place your hope in the promise of the God who cannot lie and let His truth begin to shape your life?
cautions: Do not present election as a closed list that makes the gospel call meaningless; Paul preaches so that the chosen may come to faith.
Do not imply that good works earn eternal life; they are the fruit of truth received by faith.
Do not use the Cretan quotation to stereotype any people group.

reflectionQuestions: Does the truth I know actually lead me toward godliness, or have I settled for knowing without becoming?
When my circumstances are unsettled, do I rest my hope on the God who cannot lie?
Which of the qualities required of elders most exposes an area where I need God’s grace to grow?
How do I respond when sound teaching corrects me, and do I receive it as healing rather than attack?
In what part of my life might my works be contradicting what my lips profess about God?
